config.title: Counter App

intro.title: Counter App
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Counter App using React and TypeScript. You will learn how a React component can remember values, respond to button clicks, and update what appears on the screen. We will go one step at a time, with beginner-friendly guidance throughout.
intro.usecase: The counter pattern appears in many real-world apps: product quantity selectors, likes, votes, unread counts, and dashboard widgets. By learning this pattern, you practice the core building blocks of interactive UI: state, events, and rendering.

objectives: Recognize that React components use state to remember values
Initialize and manage component state using the useState hook
Understand that state can be typed in TypeScript for safety
Create beginner-friendly event handlers for button interactions
Render changing values on screen using JSX curly braces
Connect button clicks to state updates with onClick handlers
Assemble a complete functional counter component step by step

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: React components do not remember changing values automatically. The hook that helps a component store a value is useState. Now import React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.thinkPrompt: Which React hook helps a component store a value that can change?
steps.anchor: Correct — useState is the hook used to store changing values in a component.
steps.whyThisMatters: Before a component can use React features like state, it must import what it needs.
steps.hint: Use one import statement to bring in both React and useState from 'react'.
progressiveHints: You need the word import.
React should be imported too.
Put useState inside curly braces.
Example shape: import React, { something } from 'react';
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and one named item from the same package
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: React and useState are available at the top of the file.
successCriteria: React is imported from 'react'.
useState is imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice work — React and useState are now available to use.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure both React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Not quite yet. Import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the Counter component
steps.instruction: A React component is a function that returns JSX. Now create a functional component named Counter that returns JSX.
steps.thinkPrompt: Which of these best describes a basic React component?
options: A variable that stores a string
A CSS rule for styling HTML
steps.anchor: Correct — a basic functional React component is a function that returns JSX.
steps.whyThisMatters: We need a component to hold our counter logic and UI.
steps.hint: Define something named Counter, and make sure it returns JSX such as a div or heading.
progressiveHints: Name the component Counter.
It can be a function declaration or an arrow function.
It must return JSX.

A simple starting point is return
;
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the Counter component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A Counter component exists and returns JSX.
successCriteria: A functional component named Counter is defined.
The component returns JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great — you now have a Counter component to build inside.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Make sure the component is named Counter and returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component is not set up correctly yet. Create a component named Counter that returns JSX.

steps.title: Initialize counter state with TypeScript
steps.instruction: Inside the Counter component, create a state variable named count. It should use useState, choose an appropriate TypeScript type, and initialize it to the starting value.
steps.thinkPrompt: We want to store a number that begins at 0. Which version fits that goal best?
steps.anchor: Correct — this tells React to store a counter value, and the starting value is the counter's initial value.
steps.whyThisMatters: The counter needs a value to track, and that value must live in component state.
steps.hint: Use array destructuring to get the state value and updater function from useState.
progressiveHints: The value should be named count.
The updater should be named setCount.
Use angle brackets for the type: <number>.
The starting value should be the counter's initial value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Typed state in React with TypeScript
const [value, setValue] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component has a typed count state initialized to the starting value.
successCriteria: useState is used inside the component.
The state variable is named count.
The state is typed appropriately.
The initial value is set to the starting value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice — your component can now remember the counter value.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the correct type for the counter's current value and initializing it to the starting value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state setup is missing or incorrect. Create a properly-typed counter state and initialize it to the starting value.

steps.title: Define increment handler function
steps.instruction: Inside the Counter component, define a function named handleIncrement that increases count by 1.
steps.thinkPrompt: When a user clicks an Increment button, what should happen to count?
steps.anchor: Correct — an increment action means the current number increases by 1.
steps.whyThisMatters: Buttons become useful only when they are connected to logic that changes state.
steps.hint: Create a function that calls setCount with count + 1.
progressiveHints: Name the function handleIncrement.
Use the updater function setCount.
The new value should be count + 1.
Place the function inside the Counter component.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleIncrement function updates the count state by 1.
successCriteria: A function named handleIncrement is defined.
The function calls setCount.
The updated value is count + 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice — you’ve connected a user action to a state update.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure handleIncrement calls setCount(count + 1).
steps.feedbackWrong: The increment function is missing or incorrect. Define handleIncrement and update count by 1.

steps.title: Add main container structure
steps.instruction: Replace null in the return statement with a div container that will hold the counter UI.
steps.thinkPrompt: If a component needs to show multiple UI pieces together, what is a simple root wrapper to start with?
steps.anchor: Correct — a div is a simple container element that can hold other UI parts.
steps.whyThisMatters: We need a visible root container before adding text and buttons.
steps.hint: Return a div as the root JSX element.
progressiveHints: Replace null.
Use return (...).
Start with a div opening tag.
Close the div properly.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns a div instead of null.
successCriteria: The component no longer returns null.
The component returns a JSX div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great — the component now has a visible container to build inside.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Make sure the component returns a div instead of null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a div container, not null.

steps.title: Display the current count value
steps.instruction: Inside the returned div, add a paragraph element that displays the current count using JSX curly braces.
steps.thinkPrompt: How do we show a JavaScript value like count inside JSX?
steps.anchor: Correct — JSX uses curly braces to display JavaScript values.
steps.whyThisMatters: State becomes visible to the user only when we render it in the UI.
steps.hint: Use a p tag and place count inside curly braces.
progressiveHints: Add a paragraph element inside the div.
Write some text before the value if you want.
Use {count} to render the variable.
Make sure the paragraph has opening and closing tags.
steps.analogousExample:
// Showing a state value in JSX

Current value: {someState}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI shows the current count value in a paragraph.
successCriteria: A paragraph element is added inside the div.
The paragraph displays count using JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice — the current count is now visible on screen.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure count appears inside a paragraph using curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The count display is missing or incorrect. Add a p tag and render the count variable inside JSX braces.

steps.title: Add increment button with click handler
steps.instruction: Inside the returned div, add a button with the text 'Increment' and connect its onClick event to handleIncrement.
steps.thinkPrompt: How do we connect a button click to a function in React?
steps.anchor: Correct — React uses onClick with curly braces to connect a button to a function.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is how user interaction triggers a state change.
steps.hint: Add a button and wire its onClick prop to handleIncrement.
progressiveHints: Use a button element.
The visible button text should be Increment.
Use the onClick prop.
Set it equal to handleIncrement inside curly braces.
steps.analogousExample:
// A button connected to a handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI includes an Increment button that increases count when clicked.
successCriteria: A button is added inside the div.
The button text is Increment.
The button uses onClick={handleIncrement}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great — the user can now click to increase the count.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Make sure the button text is Increment and its onClick is set to handleIncrement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not wired correctly. Add a button with text Increment and onClick={handleIncrement}.

steps.title: Add decrement and reset buttons with handlers
steps.instruction: Now add two more buttons inside the div: one labeled 'Decrement' that uses handleDecrement, and one labeled 'Reset' that uses handleReset. Also define both handler functions inside the component.
steps.thinkPrompt: If one button lowers the count and another returns it to the start, what should those actions do?
options: Decrement should subtract 1, and Reset should set count back to 0
Decrement should add 1, and Reset should remove the component
Both buttons should do the same thing
steps.correctOption: Decrement should subtract 1, and Reset should set count back to 0
steps.anchor: Correct — decrement lowers the value, and reset returns it to the starting value.
steps.whyThisMatters: A useful UI often supports multiple actions on the same piece of state.
steps.hint: Create handleDecrement and handleReset, then connect them to two buttons.
progressiveHints: handleDecrement should call setCount(count - 1).
handleReset should call setCount(0).
Add a button with text Decrement.
Add a button with text Reset.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI has Increment, Decrement, and Reset buttons, each connected to the correct behavior.
successCriteria: A handleDecrement function is defined and updates count to count - 1.
A handleReset function is defined and updates count to 0.
A Decrement button uses onClick={handleDecrement}.
A Reset button uses onClick={handleReset}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent — your counter now supports increasing, decreasing, and resetting.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress. Check that both handlers exist and both buttons use the correct onClick functions.
steps.feedbackWrong: The decrement/reset logic is incomplete or incorrect. Define both handlers and wire both buttons properly.
